summary: Pre-prod correctness cluster review (A6-A9) with adversarial verification

result.summary: Re-verified the original 2026-06-14 "Stripe period drift" critical: it is genuinely fixed. current_period_end/start are read straight from Stripe's payload (item.current_period_* with a legacy top-level fallback) via epochSecsToDate = new Date(secs*1000) — no local computation, no timezone math, no off-by-one; and currentPeriodEnd is display-only (the effective-plan SQL gates access on status + graceUntil, never on the period date), so it can't wrongly grant/deny. Webhook signature is verified on every inbound before any state mutation; duplicate delivery is deduped by Redis SETNX on event.id plus a durable stripe_webhook_events row, and the durable row is written before the dedup lock so a dropped-lock delivery is still recoverable. BILL-1 is handled: /webhooks/stripe is in the SystemModeMiddleware ALWAYS_PASS list, so maintenance/read_only/out_of_order never 503s an inbound webhook. The STRIPE-RETRY sweep correctly uses a sweep-private lock (stripe:retry-sweep:<id>, 300s TTL) rather than the controller's 30-day dedup key, so it can rescue crash-recovery rows. syncStripeSubscription has a monotonic stale-replay guard on currentPeriodStart. Admin set-plan/set-paid-until are owner-gated (role re-read live from DB). Self-serve endpoints take tenant id from server-resolved context, no cross-tenant. The grace-window anchoring (anchor to first failure, don't slide on dunning redelivery) is implemented in both the invoice and subscription.updated paths. Quota interceptor and plan guard are fail-CLOSED (any resolver error throws, never passes). I found two real gaps the prior audits missed: (1) handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted has NO stale-replay/subscription-id guard, so a replayed old delete event can clobber a newer active re-subscription on the same Stripe customer; (2) the effective-plan cache TTL is clamped to override expiry (PQF-3) but NOT to graceUntil / paidUntil, so a lapsed grace or manual paid-until over-grants paid features for up to the full cache TTL.

findings.title: STRIPE-RETRY-STALE-REPLAY gap: subscription.deleted has no id/monotonic guard — a replayed stale delete clobbers a newer re-subscription
findings.file: apps/api/src/billing/billing.service.ts:599-625 (handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted); guard exists only at :549-560 in syncStripeSubscription; sweep at apps/api/src/jobs/stripe-retry.job.ts:52-60,132-134
findings.evidence: handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted resolves the tenant by customer id only — `const billing = await controlDb.billingAccount.findFirst({ where: { stripeCustomerId: payload.customer } })` — then UNCONDITIONALLY downgrades: `controlDb.subscription.update({ where:{tenantId}, data:{ planId: starter.id, status:'canceled', stripeSubscriptionId:null, currentPeriodStart:null, ... } })`. It never checks that `payload.id` matches the currently-stored `existing.stripeSubscriptionId`. By contrast syncStripeSubscription guards out-of-order events: `if (existing?.stripeSubscriptionId === payload.id && existing.currentPeriodStart != null && nextPeriodStart != null && nextPeriodStart.getTime() < existing.currentPeriodStart.getTime()) { ...return; }`. The retry sweep re-dispatches any row with `processedAt:null` AND (`error not null` OR stale `receivedAt`), and its dispatch() routes customer.subscription.deleted straight back into handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted with the original payloadJson — bypassing the controller's 30-day Redis dedup (the sweep uses its own private lock).
findings.impact: Data-integrity / wrongful loss of paid access. Scenario: tenant cancels sub_A → Stripe sends customer.subscription.deleted(sub_A) which transiently errors (DB blip) and is persisted with error set; the tenant then re-subscribes → customer.subscription.created(sub_B) processes and the tenant is active+paid on sub_B; the stripe-webhook-retry sweep later replays the errored delete event for sub_A, and because there is no id check it downgrades the tenant to Starter/canceled, nulls stripeSubscriptionId/period, and (for paid plans) revokes desktop access and paid features even though Stripe considers sub_B fully active. Self-heals only on the next live subscription.* event for sub_B, leaving a window of wrongful denial and a desync between Stripe and local state.
findings.fix: Add the same monotonic/id guard to handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted: read the existing subscription row and bail (log + return) when `existing.stripeSubscriptionId` is set and does NOT equal `payload.id` (the delete is for a stale/superseded subscription). Only downgrade when the deleted id is the one we currently track (or when we track none).

findings.title: Effective-plan cache TTL not clamped to graceUntil / paidUntil — lapsed grace or manual paid-until over-grants paid features for up to the full cache TTL
findings.evidence: The resolver SQL correctly drops access at the boundary: `OR (s.status='past_due' AND s."graceUntil" IS NOT NULL AND s."graceUntil" > NOW())` and `AND (s."billingMode" <> 'manual' OR s."paidUntil" IS NULL OR s."paidUntil" > NOW())`. But the cached blob is held for the full TTL: writeCache clamps TTL ONLY to override expiry — `if (soonestOverrideExpiry) { const secsUntilExpiry = ...; ttl = Math.max(1, Math.min(ttl, secsUntilExpiry)); }`. graceUntil, paidUntil and currentPeriodEnd never constrain the TTL. The PQF-3 comment itself admits the failure mode for the analogous override case ("nothing writes a row at the expiry instant"), and there is no scheduled job that invalidates the plan cache when grace/paidUntil lapses (registry.ts has no grace/paidUntil sweep). Default TENANT_CACHE_TTL_SEC is 300.
findings.impact: A past_due tenant whose graceUntil expires mid-cache, or a manual-billed tenant whose paidUntil expires mid-cache, keeps full paid-plan features (and passes plan/quota gates) for up to ~5 minutes (the cache TTL) past the moment access should have dropped. Bounded over-grant, not unbounded, and only on the read path — but it is the same bug class PQF-3 explicitly fixed for overrides, left unfixed for the billing boundaries that matter most.
findings.fix: Extend the TTL-clamp in loadFromDb/writeCache to also consider the soonest of graceUntil (for past_due rows) and paidUntil (for manual rows) — return them alongside soonestOverrideExpiry and clamp the cache EX to the minimum of all upcoming expiries, mirroring the existing override clamp.

findings.title: Stale test comment in stripe-retry.job.spec.ts misdescribes the sweep lock (the code is correct)
findings.evidence: The spec mock comment claims "The sweep now claims the controller's `stripe:event:<id>` SETNX lock before dispatch (STRIPE-RETRY-NO-LOCK)", but the actual sweep uses a sweep-private key `const SWEEP_LOCK = (id) => \`stripe:retry-sweep:${id}\`` with a 300s TTL — which is the CORRECT behavior (so it doesn't contend with the controller's 30-day dedup key and can rescue crash-recovery rows). The implementation matches the audit requirement; only the test comment is misleading.
findings.impact: No runtime impact. Documentation drift only — could mislead a future maintainer into 'fixing' the sweep to reuse the controller lock, which would reintroduce the crash-recovery skip the design deliberately avoids.
findings.fix: Update the spec comment to state the sweep uses its own private `stripe:retry-sweep:<id>` lock, distinct from the controller's `stripe:event:<id>` dedup key.

verdict.reason:
Independently confirmed. handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted (apps/api/src/billing/billing.service.ts:599-625) resolves the tenant by customer id alone — `controlDb.billingAccount.findFirst({ where: { stripeCustomerId: payload.customer } })` — then UNCONDITIONALLY writes the downgrade: `controlDb.subscription.update({ where:{tenantId}, data:{ planId: starter.id, status:'canceled', stripeSubscriptionId:null, currentPeriodStart:null, currentPeriodEnd:null, graceUntil:null } })`. It never reads the existing subscription row and never compares payload.id to existing.stripeSubscriptionId. The sibling syncStripeSubscription was explicitly hardened against exactly this at :549-560 (a guard whose comment is literally named STRIPE-RETRY-STALE-REPLAY) checking `existing?.stripeSubscriptionId === payload.id && ... nextPeriodStart < existing.currentPeriodStart`; the delete handler has no analogous guard, so the protection is asymmetric.

Reachability of the harmful chain is confirmed: (1) the controller persists a failed delete with `error` set on a transient error (stripe-webhook.controller.ts:109-117); (2) ensureStripeCustomer caches and REUSES the same Stripe customer id across subscriptions (billing.service.ts:676-705), so sub_A and a later sub_B share one customer and findFirst-by-customer resolves to the same tenant after re-subscription; (3) the retry sweep re-picks errored rows — `where: { processedAt: null, OR: [{ error: { not: null } }, ...] }` (stripe-retry.job.ts:52-60) — and re-dispatches customer.subscription.deleted straight into handleStripeSubscriptionDeleted with the original payloadJson (:132-134); (4) the sweep uses its own private lock `stripe:retry-sweep:<id>` (:44, :87-92), deliberately NOT the controller's 30-day `stripe:event:<id>` dedup, so the stale delete is not deduped against the live events. Result: a swept stale delete(sub_A) clobbers the active sub_B — downgrades to Starter/canceled, nulls stripeSubscriptionId and the period fields, and calls effectivePlan.invalidate, revoking paid entitlements (effective-plan only keeps access for active or in-grace past_due rows, effective-plan.service.ts:174). Self-heals only on the next live subscription.* event for sub_B, leaving a window of wrongful denial of paid access and a Stripe/local desync.

Adjusted from the claim's high to high (unchanged). Not critical: it requires a specific event ordering (delete must transiently error, then a re-subscription, then a sweep replay within 30 days), causes no permanent data loss or double-charge, and self-heals on the next live event — it is wrongful denial of paid access for a bounded window, plus desync. The proposed fix is correct and minimal: read the existing subscription and bail when existing.stripeSubscriptionId is set and != payload.id, only downgrading when the deleted id is the one currently tracked (or none is tracked), mirroring the sync-path guard.

result.summary: The return path (loans.service) and the reservation-expiry cron correctly serialize per-book hold promotion on the SAME advisory-lock key (book:<bookId>) — that pairing is sound. But the rest of the promotion machinery is NOT mutually exclusive: placeHold/import lock on a DIFFERENT key (reservation:<bookId>), and the cancel/expire admin path (resolveReservation → promoteNextHoldInTx) takes NO advisory lock at all AND promotes the queue head with an unconditional update (no status CAS), unlike every parallel implementation which uses a status='queued' compare-and-swap. A concurrent return-vs-cancel (or placeHold-vs-cancel) on the same book can therefore both promote, and the lock-free path clobbers the CAS-protected promotion, stranding a physical copy in 'reserved' with no reservation pointing at it — exactly the "copy stranded in reserved forever" failure. Two further real issues: (1) the offline circulation queue has no entry age-limit while the server idempotency record expires after 24h, opening a double-apply window for an action that actually committed before the device went offline for >24h (renew is the clean double-apply — it re-extends and re-increments renewedCount); (2) renew checks for a blocking hold outside any transaction/lock, so a hold placed in the check→update window is missed and the loan renews past it. Fine accrual is sound (single-outstanding-per-loan index + status-guarded upserts; floor-of-24h day count is intentional and matches the return path). Unit tests mock advisory locks as no-ops, so none of the lock-key / missing-CAS issues are caught by the existing suite — consistent with the audit lesson that static/test green masked a runtime concurrency hole.

findings.title: Hold promotion is not mutually exclusive across paths: cancel/expire takes no advisory lock and uses an unconditional (non-CAS) update, stranding a copy in 'reserved'
findings.evidence: The four promotion code paths use THREE different (non-overlapping) lock regimes. loans.service.returnLoan: `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended('book:${loan.copy.bookId}',0))` then promotes with a CAS: `tx.reservation.updateMany({ where: { id: head.id, status: 'queued' }, ... })`. reservation-expiry.job uses the SAME `book:${r.bookId}` key + CAS `updateMany({ where: { id: next.id, status: 'queued' } })` — these two correctly exclude each other. BUT placeHold locks a DIFFERENT key `reservation:${input.bookId}` (line 189), and resolveReservation (cancel via DELETE /reservations/:id, and admin/cron expire via POST /reservations/:id/expire) takes NO advisory lock anywhere in its `client.$transaction` (lines 316-359) and promotes via promoteNextHoldInTx, whose head update is UNCONDITIONAL: `await tx.reservation.update({ where: { id: head.id }, data: { status: 'ready', fulfilledByCopyId: candidateCopyId, ... } })` (lines 493-502) — no `status: 'queued'` guard. Concrete race (all normal librarian/cron actions): book has queued head H and a ready hold R holding copy C1. Thread A returnLoan(C2) acquires book: lock, CAS-promotes H, reserves C2. Thread B cancel(R) takes no lock, frees C1, selects the same H as head, then its unconditional update re-points H.fulfilledByCopyId to C1 (clobbering A's promotion). C2 was flipped to 'reserved' by A but no reservation now references it → permanently stranded copy. The B-vs-A pair shares no lock so they interleave freely under READ COMMITTED.
findings.impact: Data integrity / unrecoverable corruption on the running product: a physical copy can be stranded in 'reserved' with no reservation pointing at it (un-lendable until a human notices and manually fixes the status), and the promoted patron's hold can be silently re-pointed to a different copy. The queuePosition rebalance also runs twice, potentially leaving the queue inconsistent. Reachable through ordinary concurrent return + cancel/expire on a busy desk.
findings.fix: Make every per-book promotion path take the SAME advisory lock key (standardize on `book:${bookId}`) at the top of its transaction — including resolveReservation (cancel/expire) and placeHold/import (currently `reservation:${bookId}`). Additionally, change promoteNextHoldInTx's head promotion from `tx.reservation.update({ where: { id: head.id } })` to a CAS `tx.reservation.updateMany({ where: { id: head.id, status: 'queued' }, ... })` and bail (release the just-claimed copy) when count===0, matching loans.service and the expiry job.

findings.title: Offline queue has no entry age-limit but server idempotency results expire after 24h, opening a double-apply window (renew re-extends + re-increments)
findings.evidence: offline-queue stores entries keyed by id with `createdAt` used ONLY for sort (`.sort((a,b)=>a.createdAt-b.createdAt)`); there is no age-based pruning and MAX_REPLAY_ATTEMPTS=6 counts only 5xx, not staleness. The server's idempotency record lives for `RESULT_TTL_SEC = 24*60*60`. Comment in offline-queue.ts claims safety 'rests on idempotency keys ... even if the original request had actually reached the server before the connection dropped' — but that guarantee evaporates once the 24h Redis record expires. Sequence: original POST commits server-side, response is lost on a dropped connection, device stays offline >24h; on reconnect OfflineQueueProvider.flush re-POSTs with the same Idempotency-Key, the interceptor's SETNX now succeeds (idem:<tenant>:<method>:<path>:<key> is gone), and `next.handle()` re-runs the operation. For renew this is a clean double-apply: LoansService.renew re-reads the (still-active) loan and its CAS `updateMany({ where: { id, status:'active', renewedCount: loan.renewedCount } })` passes on the fresh state, extending dueAt and incrementing renewedCount a SECOND time. (checkout is caught by loans_one_active_per_copy; most returns by the on_loan status CAS — renew is the unprotected one.)
findings.impact: A queued circulation action that already succeeded can be applied twice after a >24h offline gap. Renew double-extends the due date and over-counts renewals past maxRenewals; an over-billed/under-tracked loan results. Precondition-heavy (lost response + >24h offline) but fully silent — the librarian sees a 'synced' toast.
findings.fix: Either (a) cap offline-queue entry age (drop entries older than RESULT_TTL_SEC on flush and warn the librarian to re-verify), keeping it strictly below the server TTL; or (b) make the server idempotency RESULT_TTL_SEC effectively unbounded for these routes / persist the dedup record durably (DB) rather than only in Redis; and add a renewedCount/dueAt-aware guard so a stale renew replay is a no-op.

findings.title: Renew checks for a blocking hold outside any transaction/lock — a hold placed in the check→update window lets the loan renew past it
findings.evidence: renew is the only state-changing loan op with NO `client.$transaction` and no advisory lock. It reads `const queuedHold = await client.reservation.findFirst({ where: { bookId: loan.copy.bookId, status: { in: ['queued','ready'] } } })` (lines 612-615) and refuses if found, then later issues a separate `client.loan.updateMany(... renewedCount CAS ...)` (lines 632-635). Between the read and the write a concurrent placeHold (which locks only `reservation:${bookId}`, a different namespace) can insert a queued hold; renew has already passed its 'no hold waiting' check and proceeds to extend dueAt. The renewedCount CAS protects against double-renew but does nothing about a hold that appeared after the hold-check.
findings.impact: A member can renew and keep a book even though someone just got in line for it, contrary to the documented policy ('you can't renew while there's an active hold'). Self-correcting over time (the hold is promoted on the next return/expiry) so no corruption — purely a fairness/policy violation in a narrow race window.
findings.fix: Wrap the hold-check and the renew CAS in a single transaction that first takes the per-book advisory lock (same `book:${bookId}` key as the promotion paths), so a concurrent placeHold serializes against the renew decision.

findings.title: Idempotency replay does not re-assert the original HTTP status code (cosmetic; not a correctness bug)
findings.evidence: On a winning claim the interceptor stores only `{ body }` (line 84) and on replay returns `of(parsed.body)` (line 102), letting Nest apply the ROUTE's default status to the replay rather than the original response's status. For these routes all success responses are 200/201 so the replayed status matches; and the same-key/different-body case correctly replays the original result (true idempotency-key semantics, not a body-hash mismatch error) which is acceptable for a trusted librarian client. Noted only because a future route returning a dynamic status would replay the wrong code.
findings.impact: None today — all four circulation routes return a fixed success status, so replays are correct. Latent risk if a variable-status route is later decorated with this interceptor.
findings.fix: Optionally persist and restore the original status code alongside the body on replay; document that the interceptor assumes a fixed success status per route.

verdict.reason:
Independently confirmed. The cancel/expire path (reservations.service.ts resolveReservation, lines 283-364) wraps its work in client.$transaction (lines 316-359) with NO pg_advisory_xact_lock anywhere, and delegates promotion to promoteNextHoldInTx, whose head update at lines 493-502 is `tx.reservation.update({ where: { id: head.id }, data: { status:'ready', fulfilledByCopyId: candidateCopyId, ... } })` — unconditional, no `status:'queued'` CAS guard. The other three promotion paths all guard: loans.service.ts returnLoan (line 418) takes `book:${bookId}` advisory lock + CAS `updateMany({ where:{ id:head.id, status:'queued' } })` (line 434); reservation-expiry.job.ts (line 112) takes the SAME `book:${bookId}` lock + CAS at line 165; placeHold (line 189) takes `reservation:${bookId}` (a different key) but is internally safe via its liveCount-under-lock check. So cancel/expire shares no lock with the return/expiry paths.

Race verified under READ COMMITTED: book has queued head H + ready hold R holding copy C1. Thread A returnLoan(C2) holds the book: lock, CAS-promotes H to ready with fulfilledByCopyId=C2 and flips C2 on_loan→reserved. Thread B cancel(R) takes no lock; its promoteNextHoldInTx does a plain findFirst that can read H as still 'queued' before A commits, then issues an unconditional UPDATE WHERE id=H which blocks on A's row lock; after A commits, B's update does NOT re-check status (no CAS) and clobbers H.fulfilledByCopyId back to C1, succeeding because B freed C1 to 'available' earlier in its own tx so B's copy-claim CAS passes. Net result: C2 was flipped to 'reserved' by A but no reservation now references it → a physical copy permanently stranded in 'reserved' (un-lendable until manual repair), and the promoted patron's hold is silently re-pointed to a different copy. The CAS guard present in the other two paths would, after unblocking, see status='ready' and update 0 rows, bailing safely — which is exactly what's missing here. The duplicated queuePosition rebalance also runs in both txns.

Severity high (not critical) is appropriate: it is genuine data-integrity corruption on the running product reachable via ordinary concurrent return + cancel/expire at a busy desk, but it requires a specific concurrent interleaving (a precondition/timing window) rather than occurring on every operation, and the damage is a single stranded copy that a human can manually correct rather than unbounded/cascading corruption. The proposed fix (standardize on `book:${bookId}` lock across resolveReservation/placeHold and convert promoteNextHoldInTx's head update to a CAS updateMany that releases the claimed copy on count===0) is correct and matches the already-proven pattern in the sibling paths.

result.summary: The import pipeline is, on the whole, defensively built: MARC binary slicing clamps offsets and tolerates missing terminators, fast-xml-parser 5.8.0 is used with safe defaults (no DTD/external-entity processing, so no XXE on MARCXML), custom-field keys are locked to /^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{1,49}$/ (no __proto__ prototype pollution), int4/money ranges are pre-checked, references are tenant-scoped via the per-job tenant client, and a crash-recovery sweep prevents wedged batches. BUT the headline zip-bomb defense the prompt asked me to re-verify is NOT actually effective, and the column cap that backstops it is missing on the CSV/TSV/MARC path. Two real OOM/DoS vectors remain, plus a low-severity transform crash/data-corruption bug. The recurring theme matches the audit's warning: the comments confidently claim a defense ("reject pathological dimensions BEFORE materializing", "guards against zip-bombs") while the actual code applies the check too late (xlsx) or not at all (CSV columns). All findings are owner/admin-reachable (the import API is role+feature gated), but the worker is shared by all tenants and all five background queues, so a single malicious upload has cross-tenant blast radius.

findings.title: xlsx decompression bomb OOMs the shared worker — dimension check runs AFTER exceljs fully inflates every zip entry
findings.evidence: parseXlsx calls `await wb.xlsx.load(ab)` (line 43) and ONLY THEN checks colCount/rowCount against IMPORT_MAX_COLUMNS/ROWS (lines 52-72). The comment at lines 55-60 admits 'exceljs has already parsed the model by here'. exceljs 4.4.0 (node_modules/.pnpm/exceljs@4.4.0/.../lib/xlsx/xlsx.js:279-308) iterates every zip entry and does `content = await entry.async('string')` — fully inflating each entry (sheet1.xml, sharedStrings.xml) into a single JS string with NO decompression-size limit — before the worksheet/sharedStrings SAX parse even builds the row model. The 64MB Multer cap (IMPORT_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES) bounds only the COMPRESSED file; a deflate stream reaches ~1000:1, so a 64MB xlsx can inflate to tens of GB inside load(). import.constants.ts:13-16 and xlsx-parser.ts:55-60 both claim this is the zip-bomb defense, but the check is unreachable before the OOM.
findings.impact: A single crafted xlsx (owner/admin upload, validate OR commit phase) exhausts the worker heap during exceljs load(). V8 aborts the process on OOM — uncaughtException in worker.ts:275 cannot catch it. worker.ts runs the import, email, scheduled-jobs, maintenance, and export consumers in ONE process (lines 149-199), and the import worker is concurrency 1 (import-worker.ts:263). So one upload simultaneously kills email delivery, reservation-expiry/Stripe-retry cron, exports, and all queued imports for EVERY tenant. Cross-tenant denial of service.

findings.title: User-supplied multiSeparators is interpolated into a character class without escaping '-', causing whole-batch crash or silent data mangling
findings.evidence: splitMulti builds `new RegExp('[' + separators.replace(/[.*+?^${}()[\]\\]/g,'\\$&') + ']')`. The escape set omits '-'. Verified at runtime: multiSeparators='z-a' throws `Invalid regular expression: /[z-a]/: Range out of order in character class`, and multiSeparators='a-z' silently builds `[a-z]` so splitMulti('Hello World','a-z') returns ['H','W'] — splitting on every letter instead of the literal chars a, -, z. multiSeparators flows in unvalidated except `typeof === 'string'` (import.service.ts:319 cleanOptions). The throw is uncaught in mapRow→applyTransform (row-mapper.ts:136) and propagates to executeImport (runner.ts:55, no per-row try/catch) up to the worker catch (import-worker.ts:198), failing the ENTIRE batch rather than one row.
findings.impact: Self-inflicted (owner/admin sets the mapping option), so low severity. findings.fix: Add '-' to the escaped character set (`/[-.*+?^${}()[\]\\]/g`), or build the alternation from individually-escaped single characters rather than a character class. Wrap the RegExp construction in try/catch and surface a precise per-field issue instead of letting it abort the run.

findings.title: Verified safe: MARCXML XXE, prototype pollution, MARC binary length-field trust, error-message leakage
findings.evidence: fast-xml-parser 5.8.0 (confirmed in node_modules/.pnpm) is invoked with no processEntities/DTD options (lines 142-149), so external entities and DOCTYPE are not resolved — no XXE on the MARCXML path. findings.impact: None — these are the vectors the prompt asked to re-verify and they hold up. Documented so the audit trail shows they were actually checked at the code/version level, not assumed.
findings.fix: No change required. Optionally tighten dbIssue's fallback (line 99) to a generic message so a Prisma error string can never leak schema internals to a tenant.

verdict.reason: Independently confirmed; could not refute. exceljs 4.4.0 load() inflates every zip entry fully before any size guard. In node_modules/.pnpm/exceljs@4.4.0/.../lib/xlsx/xlsx.js:280-308, load() iterates `Object.values(zip.files)` and for each non-media entry runs `content = await entry.async('string')` (line 308) — materializing the entire decompressed entry (sheet1.xml, sharedStrings.xml) into one JS string with NO decompression-size or ratio cap (JSZip imposes none). This all happens inside `await wb.xlsx.load(ab)` at apps/api/src/import/parsers/xlsx-parser.ts:43, which runs BEFORE the colCount/rowCount checks at lines 61-72. The code comment at lines 57-60 itself concedes "exceljs has already parsed the model by here," so IMPORT_MAX_COLUMNS/ROWS are unreachable as a zip-bomb defense. The only upstream guard is Multer's 64MB cap (import.controller.ts:70, IMPORT_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES), which bounds the COMPRESSED upload only; deflate ratios of ~1000:1 let a 64MB file inflate to tens of GB. The worker.ts:275 uncaughtException handler cannot catch a V8 heap-OOM, which aborts the process directly. Net: a crafted xlsx OOMs the shared worker, a cross-tenant DoS. ONE mitigating fact the claim understates: this is NOT unauthenticated — import.controller.ts:47-49 requires an authenticated owner/admin role plus the bulk_import_enabled feature, so the attacker must be a tenant admin. That precondition is exactly why this is high, not critical: serious, cross-tenant, ops-impacting (kills billing retries + reservation expiry for all tenants), but gated behind an authenticated privileged role. No lock, guard, or idempotency prevents it; precondition is reachable; the auditor did not misread.

verdict.reason:
CONFIRMED. The IMPORT_MAX_COLUMNS (=512) cap is enforced ONLY in the xlsx parser (apps/api/src/import/parsers/xlsx-parser.ts:61-65), and its own comment states the cap exists specifically to stop a small upload from "expand[ing] to a sheet with millions of rows/columns — building the full string matrix would OOM the worker." That defense is entirely absent for CSV/TSV and MARC: csv-parser.ts -> tabular.ts:buildTableFromMatrix and marc-parser.ts:recordsToTable build their columns array purely from the data (widest-row / union-of-keys) with no column bound. The worker re-checks rows (import-worker.ts:111 `table.rows.length > IMPORT_MAX_ROWS`) but never columns.

Amplification is real and large. Upload is hard-capped at 64MB (IMPORT_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES, enforced by multer in import.controller.ts:70). A 64MB CSV of single-char comma-separated columns yields ~33M columns. tabular.ts:53-60 builds a 33M-entry ParsedColumn[]; normalizeHeaders (tabular.ts:10-24) builds a 33M-entry Map; csv-parser.ts:tokenize first materializes the entire matrix (the maxRows cap at tabular.ts:69 only limits row COUNT, applied after `widest` and `columns` are computed). Estimated live set 1.5-2GB+ stacked, exceeding the default V8 heap (no --max-old-space-size set; worker run via `tsx src/worker.ts`).

Independently reproduced: running the exact normalizeHeaders + columns-build logic on ~6M single-char columns (~12MB-equivalent, well under the 64MB cap) under --max-old-space-size=512 produced a fatal V8 "heap out of memory" abort. Notably normalizeHeaders disambiguates duplicate labels (a, a_2, a_3...), so even identical column names manufacture N distinct growing strings, worsening the blast.

Blast radius confirmed: worker.ts hosts all five BullMQ consumers (email, scheduled, import, maintenance, export) in ONE process for ALL tenants. A heap OOM is a SIGABRT, not a catchable uncaughtException/unhandledRejection, so it bypasses the graceful-drain handlers (worker.ts:271-278) and kills every queue across every tenant until the orchestrator restarts.

Precondition reachable: any owner/admin of a tenant with bulk_import_enabled (import.controller.ts:48-49). The upload-time preview even byte-slices CSV/TSV to 256KB (import.service.ts:56-59), so the wide file passes preview and detonates later in the worker on the full buffer.

Adjusted to HIGH (not critical): it is an availability/DoS issue requiring an authenticated privileged tenant user, with no data loss, double-charge, or cross-tenant data exposure. The CSV/TSV vector is the clear, trivially-weaponizable path; MARC is a weaker variant (needs many distinct tag$code records). Fix as proposed: enforce IMPORT_MAX_COLUMNS on `widest`/`order` before allocating columns/cells in buildTableFromMatrix and recordsToTable, and ideally bound tokenize to maxRows+1.

result.summary: The worker subsystem is in good shape on the items the prior audits hardened: graceful shutdown has a bounded 25s deadline that force-exits (REL-03), the prod compose healthcheck probes /readyz (real queue+Redis liveness, not an always-200), unhandledRejection/uncaughtException both drain instead of silently killing the loop, the SMTP driver has connect/greeting/socket timeouts, the new Resend HTTP driver has a 15s AbortSignal timeout, throws (rather than crashes) on non-2xx/429 so BullMQ applies exponential backoff, and never logs the API key. The rate limiter keys on X-Real-IP which Caddy overwrites from CF-Connecting-IP behind a Cloudflare-only firewall (not spoofable in this topology), and signup buckets fail closed. Per-tenant sweeps correctly pin connection_limit=1 and use status-guarded CAS updates, so no cross-tenant write or non-idempotent-on-retry issue was found there. The real gap the prior audits MISSED is the email outbox's durability promise: a cold-start / pending-row recovery scan is documented in THREE places (email-worker.ts comment, schema @@index comment, and the row-back-to-pending logic) but is never implemented — unlike imports, which do have an onModuleInit recovery sweep. Combined with a transient Redis failure during queue.add (the producer creates the DB row first), or a crash that outlives BullMQ's stalled-job retries, an outbox row can strand in pending/sending forever with no job to drain it. Two lower-severity correctness issues round it out: the idempotency PENDING marker can expire mid-handler, and the email worker re-sends on a crash between provider-send and the delivered DB write.

findings.title: Email outbox has no cold-start / pending-row recovery scan despite being documented in 3 places — stranded rows are never re-delivered
findings.evidence: email-worker.ts comment: "On step 4b ... the row going back to `pending` is just so a cold-start recovery scan can see it as 'still owed.'" The schema documents the same: "Worker polls `WHERE status='pending' AND scheduledFor <= now()`; ... this index is the cold-start recovery path." But the worker NEVER polls the table — `startEmailWorker()` only creates a BullMQ `new Worker(...)`; there is no onModuleInit/startup scan and no periodic sweep over EmailOutbox (grep for status:'pending'/'sending' recovery in src/email returns only the write sites). Contrast import-queue.service.ts:67 which DOES have `onModuleInit` cold-start recovery + a periodic `sweepStuckBatches`. Two concrete strand paths: (1) EmailService.enqueue (email.service.ts:98-137) creates the DB row FIRST, then `queue.add`; a transient Redis blip on `queue.add` throws after the row is committed pending — caught per-tenant in member-notifications.job.ts:151-154 and logged as failed, leaving a pending row with no job. (2) A worker crash that outlives BullMQ's stalled-job retry budget removes the job (removeOnComplete/Fail) while the row is still pending/sending.
findings.impact: The durable-outbox guarantee the design rests on is broken in exactly the failure modes the outbox exists to survive. Hold-ready / overdue / password-reset / support-session emails can be silently lost (row stuck pending forever, never retried) after a Redis hiccup during enqueue or a worker crash mid-flight. No alarm fires — the row just sits. For password-reset and support-key emails this is a user-facing lockout/security-notice loss.
findings.fix: Implement the documented recovery: on worker boot and on a periodic timer, scan `EmailOutbox WHERE status IN ('pending','sending') AND scheduledFor <= now()` (the @@index([status, scheduledFor]) already exists) and re-add a BullMQ job (jobId = row.id, so it dedups with any live job) for each, plus age-out 'sending' rows stuck past a threshold back to 'pending'. Mirror import-queue.service.ts's onModuleInit + setInterval(unref) pattern.

findings.title: Idempotency PENDING marker (60s TTL) can expire while the handler is still running, letting a concurrent duplicate re-run a non-idempotent circulation op (double fine/return)
findings.evidence: `PENDING_TTL_SEC = 60`. On a won claim the handler runs and only on the success `tap` is the key overwritten with the 24h result (lines 80-86). If the handler takes longer than 60s — a slow tenant DB, a contended advisory lock in the loans return/promotion transaction, or a slow checkout — the `__pending__` key EXPIRES mid-flight. A duplicate request (the offline circulation queue replaying, or an impatient double-submit) then SETNX-succeeds because the key is gone (line 69 returns 'OK'), wins its OWN claim, and re-runs the handler. The interceptor's stated purpose (header doc lines 31-32) is to stop "a returned-twice double fine".
findings.impact: Under DB slowness or lock contention, the exact double-action the interceptor was built to prevent (return-twice double fine, double checkout) can still occur on the offline-replay / double-submit path. Low frequency (needs a >60s handler) but it defeats a data-integrity guard on money-affecting routes.
findings.fix: Either (a) raise/refresh the pending TTL while the handler runs (periodic PEXPIRE / longer PENDING_TTL_SEC sized to the route's worst-case latency), or (b) make the protection robust to a lost lock by ensuring the underlying loan/fine writes are themselves keyed for idempotency. At minimum set PENDING_TTL_SEC comfortably above the slowest expected circulation transaction.

findings.title: Email worker re-sends on a crash between provider send and the 'delivered' DB write (at-least-once with no provider-side dedup)
findings.evidence: processOne only short-circuits when `row.status === 'delivered' || 'dead'` (line 111). The flow flips the row to 'sending' (line 115), calls driver.send (line 121), THEN writes 'delivered' (line 128). If the worker crashes (or is force-exited by the 25s shutdown deadline) after driver.send succeeds but before line 128, BullMQ's stalled-job recovery re-delivers the job; the row is still 'sending', so processOne proceeds and re-sends. No Idempotency-Key / dedup is sent to Resend or SMTP.
findings.impact: A patron/library can receive a duplicate of any outbox email (overdue nag, hold-ready, password reset) after a worker crash or a forced shutdown that interrupts an in-flight send. At-least-once email is generally tolerable, so impact is limited to occasional duplicate mail.
findings.fix: Send a stable idempotency token to the provider (Resend supports an Idempotency-Key header; SMTP can reuse a stable Message-ID derived from the outbox id) so the provider dedups a re-sent row, or accept and document the at-least-once semantics.

findings.title: Scheduled-jobs runner shares one Redis connection between the BullMQ Queue (producer) and the blocking Worker
findings.evidence: A single `const connection = new Redis(...)` is passed to both `new Queue(QUEUE_NAME, { connection, ... })` (line 42) and `new Worker(QUEUE_NAME, ..., { connection, ... })` (line 111). BullMQ Workers issue blocking commands on their connection; sharing that socket with a Queue producer is a documented BullMQ anti-pattern. The other workers (email/import/export/maintenance) correctly give the Worker its own socket and keep the producer Queue elsewhere.
findings.impact: Mostly benign here because the scheduled Queue is only used at boot (reconcile + register repeatables) and is otherwise idle, so production impact is minimal. Could cause command stalls if the Queue were used at runtime; flagged for correctness/consistency.
findings.fix: Give the scheduled Worker its own ioredis connection separate from the Queue's (duplicate the connection or pass a connection factory), matching the pattern in email-worker.ts / EmailService.

verdict.reason:
Independently confirmed. The email outbox is designed as a durable outbox whose recovery path is documented in 3 places (email-worker.ts:38 "a cold-start recovery scan can see it as still owed", email-worker.ts:30, and schema.prisma:723-726 "this index is the cold-start recovery path"), but no such scan exists. startEmailWorker() (email-worker.ts:49-100) only constructs `new Worker(...)` with concurrency:5 — there is no onModuleInit startup scan and no periodic setInterval sweep over EmailOutbox. worker.ts:149-155 just calls startEmailWorker(). A grep over apps/api/src/email/ for pending/sending/recovery/sweep returns ONLY the write sites (email-worker.ts:117,149), and the only other emailOutbox reader (support-session-expiry.job.ts:71) does a findMany for dedup, not re-enqueue. The scheduled-jobs registry (jobs/registry.ts) has 9 jobs, none an email-recovery sweep. By contrast import-queue.service.ts:67-74 DOES implement exactly the missing pattern (onModuleInit cold-start recovery + setInterval sweepStuckBatches).

Both strand paths are real and reachable: (1) EmailService.enqueue (email.service.ts:97-137) commits the DB row as `pending` FIRST, then calls queue.add; a transient Redis failure on queue.add throws after the row is committed — and member-notifications.job.ts:151-154 catches per-tenant errors and only logs them, leaving a pending row with no BullMQ job and nothing to find it. (2) defaultJobOptions removeOnComplete:1000 / removeOnFail:5000 (email.service.ts:81-82) plus a `sending` status that is never aged out means a worker crash past BullMQ's stalled budget strands the row.

This silently loses hold-ready/overdue/password-reset/support-session emails after a Redis hiccup during enqueue or a worker crash mid-flight — the exact failure modes the outbox exists to survive — with no alarm. I keep it at high rather than critical: prior-audit REL-04 makes /readyz 503 on a fully-dead worker (ops-detectable), the loss is recoverable manually from the durable rows, and triggering requires a Redis/crash precondition; but the user-facing password-reset/security-notice loss and the broken durability guarantee make high appropriate. The fix (onModuleInit + periodic scan of status IN ('pending','sending') AND scheduledFor<=now(), re-add jobId=row.id, age-out stuck 'sending') is correctly specified.
